issues.description: clear(s.stack) before reslicing to [:0] is redundant work
issues.detail: The defer does `clear(s.stack); s.stack = s.stack[:0]`. Once you reslice to zero length, the underlying array contents are unreachable through s.stack — any subsequent append will overwrite them. The clear() call zeroes len(stack) entries for no functional reason. The only argument for it is GC of pointer-holding Node values retained in the backing array beyond the new len; if that's the intent, do it in the opposite order: reslice first, then clear the tail you actually want to release. As written it's either dead work or in the wrong order. Pick one and comment why.

issues.description: State machine collapse loses the unsorted/walking/sorted invariant the push() switch relies on
issues.detail: Previously: unsorted -> working (children pushed) -> walking (second visit) -> sorted. Now `walking` is set on the *first* visit, before children are processed. The push() function's `case walking:` branch was designed to detect cycles back to an ancestor still on the stack — that semantic still holds, but the naming is now a lie: a node is marked `walking` while we're actually still descending into its children, not walking back up. Either keep two states with honest names (`entered`/`exited` or keep `working`/`walking`) or rename to something like `onStack`. The collapsed two-state machine works, but the next maintainer is going to have to re-derive the invariant from scratch.

issues.description: Commit message claims three fixes but the diff bundles them — THREE-PATCHES
issues.detail: The description lists: (1) reduce internal states, (2) fix non-zero elements in stack slice, (3) fix cleanup by clearing state on completion. Those are three independent changes with three independent justifications and three independent risk profiles. The state-machine collapse is a refactor. The `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` -> `s.stack[:0]` in defer is a bug fix (the old code was a no-op reslice that did nothing — `s[0:]` == `s`). The deferred clear() of state is a correctness fix for reuse across Sort() calls. Land these as three patches so a bisect can blame the right one.

issues.description: Behavioral change: state[k] = sorted now only set when yield path runs
issues.detail: Old code unconditionally set `s.state[k] = sorted` after the pop, regardless of whether `state != sorted`. New code only sets it inside the `if state != sorted` block. For a node already in `sorted` state being re-popped, the old code redundantly re-wrote `sorted`; the new code skips the write. Functionally equivalent *if* the only way to reach a popped node in `sorted` state is the duplicate-root case, but this is a real semantic change buried in what looks like a cleanup. Either call it out in the commit message or revert to the unconditional write — saving one map store isn't worth the reader's time.

issues.description: Typos in the comment you just rewrote
issues.detail: `visisted` and `if its` (should be `it's`). If you're going to rewrite the comment that documents the core invariant of the algorithm, spell-check it. The old comment was correct English; the new one isn't. This is the kind of thing that makes the maintainer-six-years-from-now wonder if the author was paying attention.

issues.description: No test added for the reuse bug being fixed
issues.detail: The PR title is 'Fix state reuse'. There should be a test that calls Sort() twice on the same Sorter, with the second call exercising state that the old code left dirty, and demonstrates the old code produces wrong output while the new code produces correct output. Without that test, the next refactor will reintroduce the bug and no one will notice.

issues.description: Good-taste win on the state collapse, if the naming gets fixed
issues.detail: Eliminating the `working` intermediate state is the right instinct — it was a special case that the two-visit DFS pattern didn't actually need, because the stack itself encodes 'have we descended yet'. That's good taste. The execution falls down only on naming. GOOD-TASTE on the structural simplification.

review.summary: The underlying instinct is right — the old code had a real bug (`s.stack = s.stack[0:]` is a no-op, leaving leftover state across reuse) and the three-state machine was one state too many. The fix lands the correct behavior. But it's submitted as one patch doing three things, the renamed state's semantics now don't match its name (a node is marked `walking` while we're descending, not walking back up), the deferred `clear(s.stack)` before reslicing to `[:0]` is either redundant or in the wrong order, and there's no regression test for the reuse bug the PR exists to fix. Verdict: NEEDS-WORK. Split into three patches, fix the state name, decide whether you're clearing the stack backing array for GC or not, add a Sort-twice test, and proofread the comment you rewrote.
